title: Lesson 62: Knowledge Graphs for Agents: Entities, Relations, and When Retrieval Gets Structured
description: Inside a knowledge graph: what entities, relations, and properties are, why vector similarity fails on relationship-path and whole-corpus questions, the four-step retrieval loop, and how to tell when the graph beats plain vector memory.

questions.question: In the lesson's opening example, why did the LangChain team's demo report "4 open tickets" when a Cypher query found five?
options: The vector index was capped at four retrieved rows by design
Vector search retrieved the four most similar task chunks and the model assumed those four were the whole population, missing the rest
The query embedded the wrong text field fore quite query
The graph contained no task nodes, so the count was defaulted to four
questions.explanation: The opening says vector search retrieved the four most similar task chunks, and the LLM assumed those four were the whole population. Similarity returned text that sounds like the question, not a count of every open task.

questions.question: In the four-step knowledge graph retrieval loop from the Redis guide, what comes immediately after linking the query's entities to matching nodes in the graph?
options: Traverse the graph by generating a graph query, for example in Cypher, that walks the relationships the question needs
Re-embed the entire graph so the vector index reflects new connections
Run a whole-corpus aggregation over every node before answering
Drop any entity whose similarity score falls below the top-N threshold
questions.explanation: The loop is: extract entities, link query entities via vector search, traverse the graph with a generated graph query, then generate the response grounded in the retrieved graph context.

questions.question: Which three question shapes does the lesson say a knowledge graph genuinely beats vector memory on?
options: Relationship-path, multi-hop queries; whole-corpus aggregation questions; and dense, interconnected domains like dependency or citation graphs
Text-similarity lookups; full-text keyword searches; and linguistic paraphrase recall
Standalone fact questions; single-document summaries; and token-length optimization targets
Image retrieval; numeric range filters; and fuzzy date matching across logs
questions.explanation: The lesson lists three shapes where resemblance fails and the graph wins: relationship-path/multi-hop queries, whole-corpus questions like top-themes-in-tickets, and dense, interconnected domains where everything looks similar to everything else.
